subject: Critical Thinking
title: Burden of Proof: Who Has to Prove What?
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Burden of Proof: Who Has to Prove What?.

hook.text: 'Prove there's no invisible dragon in my garage.' You can't. Does that mean the dragon exists? Of course not.

buildup.text: Burden of proof: the obligation to provide evidence rests on the person making the claim, not the person questioning it.

discovery.text: Hitchen's razor: 'What can be asserted without evidence can be dismissed without evidence.' No proof offered, no proof.

twist.text: Burden-shifting is a common trick: 'Prove I'm wrong.' 'You can't prove it doesn't work.' This reverses the obligation.

climax.text: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. The bigger the claim, the heavier the burden. 'I had breakfast' vs.

punchline.text: You made the claim. You bring the evidence. That's the rule.

quiz.question: Who bears the burden of proof in an argument?

details.summary: The burden of proof falls on whoever makes a claim. Shifting the burden by saying 'prove me wrong' is a common trick that reverses the rules of rational debate.
details.whyItMatters: When the burden of proof is misplaced, unfalsifiable claims go unchallenged and productive debate becomes impossible.
takeaways: The person making the claim bears the burden of proof
Shifting the burden is a rhetorical trick, not valid reasoning

faq.question: Why can't you simply say 'prove me wrong' in a debate?
faq.answer: Asking others to disprove your claim reverses the burden of proof. You cannot prove a negative exhaustively, so this trick makes any unsupported claim appear valid by default.

faq.question: How does the burden of proof work in everyday disagreements?
faq.answer: If you claim your new diet cures headaches, you need to provide evidence. Others are not obligated to disprove it. This principle protects discussions from unfounded assertions.
